entry_points.kicker: Atlantic rain · mountain wind · patient fruit

supporting_claims.statement: The Béarn–Jurançon world makes the relationship between mountain foothills, long autumn ripening, local Manseng grapes and both dry and sweet white wine unusually legible.

Jurançon’s wet Atlantic foothills are tempered in autumn by a frequent warm, dry southerly foehn. On steep slopes and terraces, late, thick-skinned local grapes can concentrate while retaining high acidity and resisting grey rot, which helps explain how dry, sweet and late-harvest wines remain distinct paths rather than different places.

entry_points.title: How can ripeness and freshness rise together?

supporting_claims.statement: The current Jurançon specification distinguishes three white-wine paths in the same geography: Jurançon sec at no more than 4 grams per litre of fermentable sugars, Jurançon above 40 grams per litre, and Jurançon vendanges tardives above 55 grams per litre.

All Jurançon grapes are hand harvested. Successive picking passes are required except for Jurançon sec, while vendanges tardives fruit cannot be harvested before 2 November; off-vine passerillage is prohibited apart from handling within the parcel during harvest.

entry_points.title: Read Jurançon sec, sweet and late harvest side by side

entry_points.kicker: Tiny berries · serious acidity · an unexpected relative

supporting_claims.statement: Plantgrape places Petit Manseng's origin in Pyrénées-Atlantiques and describes very small berries, very high acid retention despite strong sugar concentration, vigor requiring trellising/long pruning, and very strong grey-rot resistance.

Plantgrape reports published genetic analyses indicating Petit Manseng is closely related to Savagnin; this is a closeness claim, not a resolved parent-offspring statement in the evidence captured here.

entry_points.title: Follow Petit Manseng from Jurançon back to Savagnin

entry_points.kicker: Principal, accessory, and outside the rule

supporting_claims.statement: The current Jurançon specification names Gros Manseng and Petit Manseng as principal varieties and Camaralet de Lasseube, Courbu, Lauzet and Petit Courbu as accessory varieties; the vendanges tardives mention is reserved to the two Mansengs.

entry_points.title: Five local grapes are not five interchangeable names
